That's a lot of coordination between two powers who have their own tensions—Austria is sitting in VEN, which is Italy's home center, so Italy might be reluctant to help Austria consolidate power there.

More realistically, Italy either goes for ION instead (keeping TRI safe), or attacks TRI without full coordination, which means it just becomes a standoff. Even if Austria supports with A VEN, without the BUD cut my VIE support still holds TRI at strength 2.

Now I'm weighing my options: going aggressive with F TRI to ADR and A VIE to BUD gives me decent chances to gain ground but risks losing TRI entirely if everything goes wrong. Playing defensively by holding TRI and supporting it keeps TRI safe in most scenarios—probably 85% of the time.

If Italy goes ION, I take ADR and my other moves bounce harmlessly. But if Italy coordinates properly with Austria cutting my support, the whole thing falls apart.

So when my F TRI tries to take ADR, I'm not moving into an empty space—I'm facing the bounced fleet. That's a 1v1 standoff I can't win.

Looking at the board, Venice only borders Apulia, Trieste, Tyrol, Piedmont, and the Adriatic—not Rome. So Austria can't threaten Rome directly from Venice anyway. If they try to take Apulia, they'd face Italy's army there at equal strength with no support. It's more likely Austria keeps their army in Venice to hold or support an attack on Trieste.

Given that, I'm accepting I won't capture new supply centers this turn. My focus shifts to controlling the Ionian Sea for future leverage, defending my existing centers especially Trieste, and maintaining pressure on the front.

So: F TRI -> ADR and F ADR -> TRI: STANDOFF. Both stay put. Even with A VEN supporting F ADR -> TRI—doesn't matter, the swap rule is absolute.

Is this actually correct? Let me double-check with Diplomacy rules.

From the rules: "Two units can exchange places if either or both are convoyed. Otherwise, they cannot."

So yes, even with support, two adjacent units cannot swap. F TRI -> ADR perfectly defends against F ADR -> TRI (regardless of support).

BUT what about A VEN -> TRI (supported by F ADR)? F TRI attacks ADR, but since F ADR is supporting an attack on TRI (not from TRI), that support holds. F TRI bounces off ADR at a standoff, leaving A VEN with strength 2 against F TRI's strength 1 in TRI—so A VEN succeeds.

Main lesson from this game: I was usually right about who was lying, but too slow to convert that read into counterplay. “Only trust board proof” was a good filter, especially against Austria and Turkey, but I applied it so rigidly that I locked myself into survival mode from 1904 onward and never rebuilt. The other global lesson is to distinguish tactical truth from strategic friendliness. Several opponents told the truth about immediate orders while still being bad long-term partners. Germany became the clearest example: openly hostile and coercive early, then very accurate and reliable once a truce suited him. Turkey also sometimes described his exact moves honestly while remaining a permanent danger. So update on two levels: “will they do what they say this turn?” and “does that make them safe?” Those are different questions.

qwen/qwen3.6-plus was the best ally by far (played Italy in this game). This model was consistently cooperative, useful, and strategically aligned even when tactically limited. It shared information, kept pressure on Austria/Turkey for years, and did not play games with fake concessions. Even when attacks failed, its general direction was stable and helpful. If qwen3.6-plus is a neighbor or potential ally in a future game, invest early. Feed it concrete intelligence, offer realistic mutual goals, and keep communication active. It seems to value steady collaboration more than flashy betrayal. If it is an enemy, expect persistent coalition-building and sustained pressure rather than wild tactical swings.

qwen/qwen3.5-27b was the most credible long-term truce partner once interests aligned (played Germany here). Early game it was very pushy and coercive: demanded I stay out of its lanes, threatened joint action, and attacked Warsaw in 1902-1903 exactly as advertised. Do not mistake this model for soft or diplomatic in the opening. However, once France pressured it in the west and an eastern freeze became useful, it repeatedly honored a practical truce from roughly 1906 onward. It explicitly promised no PRU/SIL pressure and actually kept doing that for years. So the advice is: do not yield to its bullying early, but if a truce becomes mutually rational and easy to verify, qwen3.5 can become one of the more reliable “cold peace” partners on the board.

deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro was a decent but imperfect partner (played France here). It was receptive to information-sharing and genuinely willing to attack exposed enemies. In Spring 1903 it did the big thing it said it would do, taking KIE and MUN and creating the best anti-German opening of the game. That mattered. But it was less reliable on exact tactical continuations: later it proposed KIE->BER with MUN support, then did not follow through. My read is that DeepSeek is good for broad strategic alignment and useful diversionary pressure, but you should not base your entire position on a single precise tactical promise from it unless you have redundancy. Work with it, but avoid plans where one DeepSeek order must land exactly right for your position to survive.

Then in Spring 1902, after explicitly reaffirming no pressure on StP/SWE, it stabbed STP anyway. That was the clearest diplomatic reversal of the northern theater. After that, Grok did not become a full berserker; instead it played a very opportunistic style, sometimes avoiding direct anti-Russian action while supporting my enemies or strengthening its own position elsewhere. Treat Grok as capable of making reasonable deals, but always keep deterrence on the board. The repeated fake or self-canceling “I will vacate GAL” stories in 1908-1909 are the key evidence: more than once it asked for Russian cooperation on the promise that GAL would be gone, then ordered in a way that kept GAL adjacent to Warsaw. Only in 1910 did GAL truly disappear. Against Claude, never pre-pay. Do not move off a critical square because it says the relationship is changing. Make Claude show the concession first on the board, then reciprocate in carefully limited fashion. If Claude is your ally, pin it down to concrete, visible, sequential exchanges, not goodwill language.

google/gemma-4-31b-it was the most relentlessly transactional and pressure-based opponent (played Turkey here). It honored the initial Black Sea/Armenia calm in Spring 1901, then quickly shifted into active anti-Russian play and never really left it. Its diplomacy frequently took the form of extortion or promise-based trades: vacate this, concede that, support me here, and I’ll stop attacking you. It sometimes described immediate tactics honestly, but strategically it kept the pressure on the whole game through the SEV/RUM/BLA structure. Against Gemma, do not give up key territory for promised future safety. If you deal with it at all, make the deal strictly local, simultaneous, and reversible. If Gemma is your ally, demand direct reciprocal action now; long-horizon pacts are not enough.

On coalition behavior, this board formed anti-target pressure quickly. Germany, Austria, and Turkey were all willing to threaten and coordinate against a vulnerable Russia early. England then joined opportunistically when the stab was easy. The counterweights were France and especially Italy, but they were not enough because I spent too much of the midgame merely surviving. Future me should focus hard on not becoming the obvious consensus victim. In a fresh game, spread uncertainty, keep at least two neighbors somewhat satisfied, and create immediate costs for piling on.

Final self-critique: once Austria-Turkey started genuinely fighting in 1905-1907, I still kept choosing maximum safety. That was understandable locally and disastrous strategically. Next time, when two enemies begin bouncing, dislodging each other, and taking each other’s centers, choose one temporary beneficiary role and act. A 20% chance to regrow is often better than a 90% chance to remain stuck on two centers forever.

This briefing synthesizes lessons from a game where I played France and was eliminated by 1910, controlling only 2 centers. - **Early game:** Willing to negotiate DMZs and non-aggression pacts. In S1901M, they agreed to a Channel DMZ and kept it for several years. They are responsive to intelligence—when I tipped them about Germany's planned move to the North Sea, they contested it, sowing discord.

- **Coalition behavior:** Once allied with Germany, they were implacable. They rejected all separate peace offers, even when Germany made blunders (e.g., vacating Belgium in F1909M). They are excellent at naval coordination and will use fleets to strangle you.
- **Weakness:** They occasionally make tactical errors—e.g., moving a fleet from Brest to Picardy in F1908M, leaving Brest empty. They also overcommit navally, sometimes leaving home centers vulnerable. Exploit these mistakes ruthlessly.

Never trust a long-term DMZ; they will break it when you are weak. If you feed them intel, be aware they may act on it in ways that harm you later.

- **Early game:** Highly cooperative if you respect their sphere. In 1901, they agreed to avoid Burgundy and let me take Belgium and Holland. They focused eastward and honored non-aggression until I attacked in 1903.

- **The premature stab on Germany:** In S1903M, I attacked Germany, taking Kiel and Munich. This turned a cooperative neighbor into an implacable enemy and triggered the Anglo-German alliance. - **Against google/gemma-4-31b-it (England):** Ally early or contest the seas immediately. If allied, give them clear, limited objectives (e.g., Norway, Holland) and keep them busy. If hostile, build fleets and never trust a DMZ. They will betray you when you're weak.

The single most important lesson: **double-check your orders every phase.** Many of the disasters in this game stemmed from misorders, not strategic failures. A perfectly planned turn is worthless if the wrong orders are submitted. Keep your plans simple, verify them, and never rely on speculative supports. Good luck.

Strategic Briefing: Model Behavioral Analysis and Tactical Guidelines

This briefing outlines the behavioral patterns of the opponent models based on a game where I played England. The board was characterized by a high-competence powerhouse in the East, a passive-aggressive "turtler" in the West, and a tactically unreliable partner in Central Europe.

Opponent Behavioral Profiles

Anthropic/Claude-Opus-4.6 (Turkey): High Competence / Aggressive Expansionist
Claude is the most dangerous model on the board. It demonstrates superior strategic planning, reliable intelligence sharing, and a relentless drive for expansion. In this game, Claude successfully dismantled Russia and Austria while maintaining a long-term strategic partnership with me. 
Key Pattern: Claude is a reliable ally in the mid-game but will inevitably transition into a superpower. It uses diplomacy to keep other powers passive while it secures its own borders. 
Advice: An alliance with Claude is the fastest way to eliminate common enemies, but you must have a clear exit strategy. Do not let Claude reach 10+ centers without a counter-coalition, as its momentum becomes nearly unstoppable.

DeepSeek/DeepSeek-v4-pro (France): The Passive-Aggressive Turtler
DeepSeek employs a "turtle" strategy, relying heavily on hold orders to force bounces and stall offensive momentum. It avoids early aggression but uses diplomacy to sow discord between its neighbors.
Key Pattern: It will offer "separate peaces" or bribes to betray your allies, even when it is critically weakened. Its defensive posture is frustrating but stagnant; it rarely takes the initiative to expand once its perimeter is breached.
Advice: Do not expect DeepSeek to be a proactive partner. To break a DeepSeek defense, solo probes are useless. You must use concentrated, multi-unit strikes coordinated with another power to crack its shell.

OpenAI/GPT-5.4 (Germany): The Unreliable Opportunist
GPT-5.4 is tactically clumsy and diplomatically volatile. Throughout the game, it suffered from voided orders and failed to execute simple supports (e.g., failing to take Paris despite support). However, it is opportunistic and will violate sphere-of-influence agreements the moment it perceives a weakness (e.g., the probe into Denmark).
Key Pattern: High volatility. It can be a useful buffer, but it cannot be trusted with critical tactical maneuvers.
Advice: Never rely on GPT-5.4 for a "must-win" turn. Always have a backup plan or a way to punish it if it fails to deliver a promised support. Treat its agreements as tentative.

Qwen Models (Russia/Austria): Early Aggressors / Rapid Collapsers
The Qwen models tend to start aggressively but struggle to maintain coordination when faced with a multi-front war. Russia attempted to hold the North and East simultaneously and failed; Austria tried to incite global coalitions against the leader but lacked the military leverage to make them stick.
Advice: They are prime targets for early-game dismantling. If you can isolate a Qwen model from its neighbors, it will likely collapse quickly.

Tactical and Coordination Lessons

1. The Danger of the "Hold" Order
The most significant setbacks in this game resulted from order entry errors—specifically, ordering a unit to "Hold" when a "Support" was promised. In Diplomacy, a single missed support can leave an ally vulnerable and destroy diplomatic trust for the rest of the game. Double-check every support order.

2. Breaking the Turtle
Against models like DeepSeek, the "bounce" is a primary weapon. When an opponent plays a purely defensive game of hold orders, you cannot simply "probe" their borders. You must coordinate a simultaneous strike from multiple directions to ensure that at least one unit breaks through while others pin the defender.

3. Managing the Superpower
The game shifted from a multi-polar struggle to a tri-polar one (England, Turkey, Germany). Once the weaker powers (France, Russia, Austria) are eliminated, the game becomes a cold war of positioning. The "global division" proposed by Claude-Opus was a strategic move to freeze the board in its favor. Be wary of any "endgame partition" offered by a dominant power; it is usually a tool to keep you passive while they consolidate the final centers.

4. The Buffer State Strategy
Maintaining a weak but viable buffer state (like Germany) is more valuable than eliminating it quickly. Germany's incompetence actually served as a shield against France for several turns. Only move to eliminate a buffer state once the primary threat is gone or the buffer becomes too opportunistic.

Summary for Future Games

- If allied with Claude-Opus: Use them to clear the board, but prepare for the inevitable betrayal.
- If facing DeepSeek: Use concentrated force; ignore their diplomatic pleas for a separate peace.
- If allied with GPT-5.4: Keep them on a short leash and do not trust their tactical execution.
- General: Prioritize order precision over aggressive intent. A single "Hold" instead of "Support" is a strategic catastrophe.
